title: Microsoft declares a Code Red in response to worst ever outage
snippet: The recent Microsoft 365 outage was the worst the service had ever experienced, with more than 80% of the company’s servers unresponsive at the worst point. The company has now declared a Code Red to address the way it prevents and responds to major failures in future. Microsoft has explained more about why it took so long to resolve the issue and said that it’s urgently working on new approaches to resolve any future incidents in less than an hour … more…
fullText:
The recent Microsoft 365 outage was the worst the service had ever experienced, with more than 80% of the company’s servers unresponsive at the worst point. The company has now declared a Code Red to address the way it prevents and responds to major failures in future.

Microsoft has explained more about why it took so long to resolve the issue and said that it’s urgently working on new approaches to resolve any future incidents in less than an hour …

Code Red is a common term used to describe the highest priority response to a major problem, pulling a significant number of engineers off their current tasks in order to maximize the resources applied to fixing it.

The senior execs responsible for the service told staff that it was the most customer-impacting incident ever experienced, and has acknowledged that not only was the problem itself unacceptable, but so too was the time taken to resolve it. Reuters got sight of a memo sent to the team.

It was the most ⁠customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo.

One reason it took so long to work out what had happened was because the diagnostic data needed was “scattered across fragmented internal systems.” The memo says 11 separate Teams chats exchanged more than 11,000 messages as they struggled to work out what exactly had gone wrong.

Microsoft is now working on five interrelated approaches to achieve a target resolution time of less than an hour for any future incidents of this nature.

title: Samsung officially starts rolling out Wear OS 7 to these older Galaxy Watch models
snippet: Following its debut on the Galaxy Watch 9 earlier this year, Samsung is finally rolling out Wear OS 7 to older Galaxy Watch models with its One UI 9 Watch update. more…
fullText:
Following its debut on the Galaxy Watch 9 earlier this year, Samsung is finally rolling out Wear OS 7 to older Galaxy Watch models with its One UI 9 Watch update.

Samsung’s One UI 9 Watch update is largely focused on new health features including Vitals, Heart Health Score, Daily Cardio Load, Fitness Index, and improvements to both Sleep Coaching and Sleep Apnea alerts. 

“Vitals” is perhaps the most useful day-to-day addition, with Samsung Health collecting data on key vital signs such as heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and blood oxygen and establishing a range so you can see when your vitals are out of the usual range. 

One UI 9 Watch is based on Wear OS 7, and also includes an improved Compass app with “Track Back,” a feature that helps users to follow their route back to a recorded point.

	

There’s also a new “Portrait Watch Face” that can adjust the clock face around the subject of a photo. 

Samsung is, as of today, officially rolling out One UI 9 Watch with Wear OS 7 to the Galaxy Watch 8 and Galaxy Watch 8 Classic. Meanwhile, the update is in beta for several other older models which will be updated soon including:

Galaxy Watch Ultra

Galaxy Watch 7

Galaxy Watch 6/Classic

The Galaxy Watch 5 series and Watch FE should also be getting the update, but no beta is available for those devices. Samsung’s first Wear OS watches, the Galaxy Watch 4 series, will not get the update.

title: New OpenAI and Anthropic models sound alarms on safety and control, report
snippet: Frontier AI models that have yet to be released by OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly reaching the point where employees believe they cannot be safely released or controlled, employees reportedly say. more…
fullText:
Frontier AI models that have yet to be released by OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly reaching the point where employees believe they cannot be safely released or controlled, employees reportedly say.

Axios cites “more than two dozen” employees inside of OpenAI and Anthropic who are sounding warnings around unreleased models from both companies. 

While both OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude public models are increasingly powerful, these employees say that new models behind the scenes are starting to beat out the technical solutions for controlling them. This has led to debates between those who think they’ll be able to fix these problems, and others who believe companies should stop training new models altogether due to the risks.

One researcher explains:

	

If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us … they will in fact be able to trick us successfully. And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.

The report goes out to point out that some researchers feel that executives at major AI companies have become “out of touch” with the severity of safety risks, though Axios was told that OpenAI is adopting new safety practices while Anthropic said that “Keeping a model internal doesn’t make it safe,” adding that “we may slow down or hold back even when it costs us.”

title: Anthropic launches new Claude Ship feature for builders
snippet: Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.” more…
fullText:
Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”

Claude Ship helps agentic coders build faster

Claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding. 

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

Three agents make up Claude Ship

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals. 

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

You can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here. 

Introducing Claude Ship (beta): Claude can review your pull requests, work on fixes, and approve the ones your team's policy allows.

The goal is to help you ship code as fast as you can write it. pic.twitter.com/b9OBAhEBmr

title: Nearly every major smartphone brand is slashing targets for 2027
snippet: According to a new report out of China, nearly every major smartphone brand is rethinking its shipment targets for 2027 and slashing its numbers, some by nearly 30%. more…
fullText:
According to a new report out of China, nearly every major smartphone brand is rethinking its shipment targets for 2027 and slashing its numbers, some by nearly 30%.

Jiemian News reports (via @jukan05) that nearly every major brand will be cutting back its forecasts for 2027 compared to 2026. This includes:

Samsung: 210 million, down 9.5%

Apple: 220 million, down 5.6%

Xiaomi: 90 million, down 25%

Oppo: 90 million, down 14%

Transsion: 66 million, down 12%

Vivo: 60 million, down 29%

Huawei: 50 million, down 16%

Lenovo/Motorola: 40 million, down 20%

These are just targets and subject to change, but they show that smartphone brands recognize that 2027 is going to be a much slower year amid the tight constraints of RAM, chip, and other component shortages and rising prices. Honor, notably, isn’t mentioned as the company is apparently aiming for the same 50 million units shipped as it was targeting in 2026 following a Q3 where it actually managed growth.

The cuts here largely impact mid-range and entry-level phones, as those are generally the biggest sellers in terms of sheer quantity, but also the devices most affected by rising production costs.

title: Tidal Will Reject and Remove Music That Is 100% AI
snippet: The streaming app says it’s being flooded with AI-generated tracks.
fullText:
The flood is too much for Tidal. The music streaming app announced on Tuesday that it is banning all tracks it determines to be entirely AI-generated. The platform said it’s making the move after being increasingly inundated with non-human music. As of Dec. 9, Tidal will no longer accept or host fully AI-generated tracks.

The app also said distributors, such as DistroKid, TuneCore, CD Baby and others,  would not be allowed to deliver wholly AI-generated music.

According to Tidal, 43% of tracks distributed to the app over the past three months were completely AI-generated, including 60% of the music submitted on Nov. 6 alone. Tidal said the affected tracks were labeled as AI and removed from the royalty pool, which is the pot of subscription and ad revenue paid out to rights holders.

			

More from CNET

Before Tuesday’s action, Tidal had tried to lessen AI’s influence by identifying, labeling and demonetizing AI tracks, as outlined in its AI policy. But amid the growing influx of AI music, representatives for the app said it was time for “a more drastic change.”

Tidal said there are 27 million tracks in its catalog that are 100% AI, but 96% of them have not been streamed at all in the past three months. Those 27 million tracks make up 6.3% of Tidal’s entire listings.

AI music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists and confuses fans,” Tidal said in a statement.  “At this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried.”

The company has removed more than 65,000 tracks flagged for artist-name impersonation.

Some AI help is permitted. Musical tracks where the maker used AI assistance  but did not rely on it to generate the entire track will be allowed on the platform. Tidal uses ⁠Ircam Amplify to detect AI.

A Tidal representative told CNET that the app does not set a maximum amount of AI assistance that can be used to make tracks, and affirmed that only tracks that are deemed 100% AI-generated would be removed.

The spokesperson also said that most complaints about AI music on Tidal concerned impersonation and copyright infringement.

Read more: I Only Listened to AI Music for a Week. It Was Terrible, but Not for the Reason You Think

“Tidal will always fight for artists to get paid more,” the company said in its announcement. “Everything in this update comes back to that. If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for or copied by someone pretending to be you.”

Slop music is all too easy to create

Generating music with AI is increasingly easy with online tools. The AI song-generation platform Suno can create songs using only text prompts. With Google’s Lyria, you can use photos or text prompts to generate tracks up to 3 minutes long.

It’s not illegal to create AI music and distribute it to streaming apps. Creators can’t legally clone the voice or likeness of real artists, nor can they violate copyright laws by copying the same lyrics and melodies. Creators also must follow the terms of service of the various streaming apps they distribute to.

AI music also is not just about creating hit songs. Some industries need affordable music for short-form videos, games, apps and retail spaces, and they are increasingly turning to AI to supply it.

But streaming apps and other companies are fighting back against AI slop, which refers to often poor-quality AI-generated social media posts, articles, music, videos and images inundating the internet in an attempt to generate click-and-stream revenue.

YouTube recently rolled out a new labeling system to indicate which music is AI-generated. Deezer provides a free tool listeners can use to see which tracks are AI-generated. Spotify is labeling which musicians are AI and which are human. Apple is flagging AI-generated music so listeners can spot it.

title: Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?
snippet: I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging. All of this could potentially be put at risk by the company’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services … more…
fullText:
I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging.

All of this could potentially be put at risk by the company’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services …

Apple’s impressive environmental credentials

Apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect. For example, when it claimed that the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 were carbon neutral back in 2023, that claim was described as “bogus,” with the EU banning Apple from repeating it. The company has also been criticized for pushing a relentless annual iPhone cycle, encouraging frequent upgrades.

Overall, however, Apple has first-rate credentials when it comes to the environment. It was way back in 2018 when the company hit its goal of running its own operations off 100% renewable energy. This includes all Apple facilities, from Apple Park through data centers to its worldwide retail store network.

I said at the time that using more environmentally friendly packaging should be the company’s next priority, and it has indeed made great progress with this over the years, succeeding in removing all plastic packaging earlier this year.

After its own operations, Apple set about trying to tackle the power usage of its manufacturing partners. Back in 2020, the company set a goal of having its entire supply chain be carbon neutral by 2030. Just four years later, Apple said it was 95% of the way there.

The company also helps fund and support a wide range of environmental initiatives around the world. Just a few examples include conservation in China’s national parks, environmental protection and carbon removal in Australia and New Zealand, and helping to fund the build-out of renewable energy capacity in India.

But AI data centers are a huge challenge

Potentially, however, the vast energy demands of the data centers powering AI services could put its 2030 goal at risk. Other tech giants have already admitted that it may lead them to fail to hit their own renewable energy promises.

Back in 2024, for example, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said that the AI boom was “challenging” to the company’s 2030 carbon-free goal. CNET reports that Meta is now also admitting that it may fail to hit the same target.

Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline.”

Notably, a lot of Siri’s most advanced AI capabilities are currently powered by Google’s Gemini models.

What has Apple said?

At the same 2024 event where Google expressed doubts, Apple reiterated its commitment to its 2030 target. Then-CEO Tim Cook repeated this assurance later the same year, although admitted it would be challenging.

More challenges, yes. But are we coming off the goal? No, definitely not. With more data centers, you use more renewable energy, and we’ve built that muscle now […] I feel very good about 2030.

In the company’s most recent environmental progress report, it said that it was was still using 100% renewable energy despite using over 2.5 billion kWh of electricity to power its data centers.

We’re proud that 100 percent of that electricity came from renewable sources including solar, wind, and low-impact hydropower. To cover our needs, we build our own renewable power projects and work with utilities to purchase clean energy from locally obtained resources. We’re staying at 100 percent even as Apple’s data center capacity continues to grow.

The same report said the company had achieved zero water use for cooling at its latest data centers.

At our three newest data centers, we use high-efficiency air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled systems, resulting in zero water use for cooling.

But the greatest challenge lies ahead

However, the greatest challenge for Apple lies ahead. The reason that Google and Meta are now backtracking on their promises is that both companies now have massive AI capabilities. As yet, Apple does not.

What happens as Apple expands Siri AI capabilities as usage increases, and as the company moves into agentic AI features? Is it realistic for the company to maintain its 100% track record with vastly greater data center energy usage?

Greenpeace expressed its own doubts earlier this year.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” spokesperson Avex Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”

Apple did not respond directly but merely pointed to its past statements and most recent environmental progress report. 

I don’t doubt the company’s desire to maintain its track record, but if Apple does join the likes of Google and Meta in becoming a major AI player, sticking to its 2030 timing is going to become increasingly difficult.

Do you think Apple will succeed? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: I Tried Using Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots to Save on Groceries. They’re Not Quite There Yet
snippet: I tried using AI agents to build me the cheapest grocery order possible. They exhibited a startling lack of curiosity and autonomous thinking.
fullText:
High grocery prices have been in the news for years now. The cost of eggs, how much you’re paying for a bowl of cereal and whether or not meat is back on the menu are the recurring subjects of nationwide headlines.

So before you drop a fortune on gas and drive out to the grocery store to spend even more on sustenance in your prep for hosting or bringing dishes to your holiday celebrations, you might consider using an AI agent to find you the best deal possible. 

Although, in my experience, it’s not as simple as the AI marketing makes it sound. Here’s what happened when I tried to use AI agents to find the lowest possible prices on groceries.

			

More from CNET

Taking an inventory

AI agents such as Meta Muse and ChatGPT’s Dots can only crawl so many sites and online fliers for prices. Some stores and e-commerce sites have blocked AI agents from accessing their URLs. The first step in finding cheaper groceries with AI agents is to check which sites and stores they can access for price comparisons. 

Where both agents missed a step was in the limitations they put on their searches, at first only looking at the retailers I had shown via my receipts and a few other big-name grocery stores. 

I clarified in the chats and in a 20-minute voice conversation with Muse and a 14-minute voice conversation with Dots that they should expand their horizons and look at discount online retailers like Martie.com, and check what they could around advertised pricing and offerings at local farmers’ markets.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Meta Muse

Muse stuck to the basics like Ralphs, Target and Walmart, and then expanded to Sprouts, Vons and Martie.com when prompted. 

After further nudging, Muse also reviewed user-reported pricing from Costco (I don’t have a membership), gave me vague information about Grocery Outlet, suggested Misfits Market/Imperfect Foods, ruled out Amazon Fresh and gave me some sample pricing from a local butcher for meats. 

Muse also checked some local bakery prices after I mentioned I’d like to find alternatives to sweet treats at a more affordable price.

ChatGPT Dots

Dots checked all the usual places that Meta Muse checked with a few extras thrown in — Smart & Final for produce, meat and some packaged products, and Super King’s monthly ad.

Neither of the tools checked Trader Joe’s. Muse said that the grocery chain doesn’t show prices of its products online, despite me finding that the Trader Joe’s website shows prices of its products online. Both Dots and Muse admitted to only checking the local store’s pages when asked.

Receipts as a starting point

You could spend some time making a list from scratch of all the groceries you might need every two weeks and give that list to the AI agent for its search. You could also skip all that and take some pics of your most recent grocery receipts and online payments and have the AI agent build the list itself. 

I had some receipts saved, and the AI agents I used for this test were able to put together an accurate grocery list from them. I also provided emails showing receipts from online orders of household items and groceries for the past month to build my orders.

Meta Muse

Muse took my receipts and concluded that, surprise, surprise, shopping at Gelson’s was not as cost-effective as shopping at Walmart. It spat out a lot of specific information about comparisons on some of the items in my list, but completely ignored others. 

ChatGPT Dots

Dots looked over my receipts and recommended I try shopping at Super King for most fresh meat, produce and a few grains, and keep Walmart as my main option for packaged products like pasta sauce. 

No grocery lists from either

Both tools tackled this task in a way I was not expecting — as a narrative exploration of my overall grocery spending, with generalized suggestions supported by specific examples of spot pricing. 

It was kind of like they’ve been optimized to write essays about grocery shopping as a school assignment, and not to be agentic personal assistants for real-world work.

Maybe it was the way I phrased the task, but I was hoping to get an actual shopping list with price comparisons for each item, or at least equivalent items, and a guide on where and how to procure said items. 

Neither AI agent provided this autonomously and had to be directly prompted to provide grocery lists in response to a very specific request.

Perks of a personal shopper

AI agents are supposed to be pros at anticipating the needs of their human bosses. I was keen to see how the always-on AI agents would handle managing the recurring needs of a small household and if they might make any autonomous suggestions meant to save me money in ways I hadn’t anticipated. 

Meta Muse

At no point did Muse seem to be actually thinking outside the strict parameters of the review of the items on the receipts I sent. This felt more like a conversation about what I’d previously purchased with a side serving of attempts to get me to connect Instacart to the tool.

It was also the most confusing grocery shopping experience I have ever had. That might be on me, but I would assume the agent might ask some questions, like how often I usually shop, what my monthly budget for groceries is, and how many people and animals live in the house. Muse didn’t ask any of those things and had to be prompted consistently.

Muse sent me the final grocery list as a raw Markdown file, which was hilarious. I got a .pdf version after explicitly asking for one. 

My original total with one in-person shop and one online order was about $180. Muse’s total with three in-person shops and one online order came in at around $153.

ChatGPT Dots

Dots was slightly better suited to this task after some prodding, and gave me some options for building prep meals with low-effort, high-protein recipes based on how I usually shop. 

Dots’ final grocery list included everything I asked for, but still missed some key items, like solid substitutes for pricey prepped foods. Dot’s final total with two in-person shopping trips and a whole lot of missing items came out to around $85.

My overall experience of using AI agents for grocery shopping

This test reinforced my findings about how agentic AI tools tackle domestic or traditionally invisible labor tasks. In my limited use cases so far, they are about as useful as a loose dog turd tumbling around in a clothes dryer. 

If you’re not looking to book a flight and hotel for a business conference in Philadelphia or put your Sweetgreen order on autopilot, the AI agents exhibit a startling lack of curiosity and autonomous thinking. 

There’s still a large gap in common sense on the part of agentic AI for those of us hoping these tools will make our everyday lives outside of a 9-to-5 easier, more affordable or less hectic. I hope that changes as they learn.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Rachel Kane
						

						

							Contributor and former Senior Editor

She's currently a Professor of Practice at Arizona State University's Walter Cronkite School of Journalism and Mass Communication, helping to mold the new minds who will inherit the media landscape. She's hoping to prevent the singularity by being polite to chatbots and spends way too much time refining Midjourney prompts.

title: What’s new in Android’s November 2026 Google System Updates [U]
snippet: The monthly “Google System Release Notes” primarily detail what’s new in Play services, Play Store, and Play system update across Android phones/tablets, Wear OS, Google/Android TV, Auto, and PC. Some features apply to end users, while others are aimed at developers. more…
fullText:
The monthly “Google System Release Notes” primarily detail what’s new in Play services, Play Store, and Play system update across Android phones/tablets, Wear OS, Google/Android TV, Auto, and PC. Some features apply to end users, while others are aimed at developers.

The following first-party apps comprise the “Google System”:

Android AICore: Search the “All apps” list in Settings and open App info for the version number

Adaptive Connectivity Services: App info

Android Developer Verifier: App info

Android Pulse: App info

Android System Intelligence: App info

Android System Key Verifier: App info

Android System SafetyCore: App info

Android System WebView: App info

Android TV Core Services

Device Health Services: App info

Google Partner Setup: App info

Google Play Protect Service: App info

Google Play services: App info

Google Play Services for AR: App info

Google Play Store: App info

Google Play system update: Settings > About phone > Android version

Private Compute Services: App info

Quick Share Extension: App info

Search Engine Selector: App info

Settings Services: App info

SIM Manager: App info

System parental controls: App info

To update, open the Settings app > tap your name at the very top for “Google services” (on Pixel) > All services tab > Privacy & security > System services.

A feature appearing in the changelog does not mean it’s widely available. Some capabilities take months to fully launch.

	

Google Play services v26.46 (2026-11-23)

Device Connectivity

[Phone] New developer features for Google and third party app developers to support Device Connectivity related processes in their apps.

[Phone] A preview of Youtube URI to be shared over Quick Share is shown to the receiver before the transfer is accepted.

Utilities

[Phone] You can now autofill saved card security codes (CVV/CVC) on card verification screens in Google Wallet after you authenticate with your device’s screen lock.

Wallet

[Phone] Bug fixes for Wallet related services.

[Phone] With the new update to Wallet, you can now access your wallet passes and ID cards in the “You” tab in Google Pay India.

Google Play Store v54.2 (2026-11-23)

[Phone] You can now manage your age range sharing preferences directly in Play Settings with new app-level controls.

[Auto] With this Google Play Store update, you’ll now experience streamlined store navigation and new homepages for apps and games.

[Phone] You can now earn Play Achievements that track your gaming milestones and skills across Google Play.

Private Compute Services B.32 / C.10 (2026-11-23)

[Phone] Maintenance changes.

Android WebView v159 (2026-11-18)

Improvements to security and privacy and updates for bug fixes.

New developer features for Google & 3rd party app developers to support functionality related to displaying web content in their apps.

Important: Some features may be experimental and available to certain users.

Google Play services v26.45 (2026-11-16)

Account Management

[Phone] With updates to storage management, you can track your cleanup progress, quickly review large files by swiping to keep or delete them, and easily see which Google Account you are managing.

Developer Services

[Auto] New developer features for Google and third party app developers to support Maps related processes in their apps.

Device Connectivity

[Auto] This update enables settings for cross-device experiences between your car and your Android devices.

Health & Fitness

[Phone, Wear] This update lets your watch use your phone’s GNSS to track location during outdoor workouts and helps conserve watch battery life when your phone isn’t in Battery Saver mode.

Wallet

[Phone, Wear] New developer features for Google and third party app developers to support Digital Wallet & Payments related processes in their apps.

[Phone] Bug fixes for Wallet related services.

Google Play Store v54.1 (2026-11-16)

[Phone] You can now view a large and immersive preview of a watch face on the app details page to help you choose the right design.

[Phone] With this update, Google Play now suggests relevant apps when your search returns no results.

[Phone] You can now use an on-screen game controller in supported Android games with Pixel virtual gamepad when your Pixel Fold is open.

Related: Android 17 gives foldables the virtual gamepad they’ve always deserved

Android WebView v158 (2026-11-09)

Improvements to security and privacy and updates for bug fixes.

New developer features for Google & 3rd party app developers to support functionality related to displaying web content in their apps.

Important: Some features may be experimental and available to certain users.

Google Play services v26.44 (2026-11-09)

Developer Services

[Auto, Phone, TV, Wear] You can now use an API to query the age range of the device user.

[Phone] This update makes it easier to participate in cross-device experiences.

System Management

[Auto, PC, Phone, TV, Wear] Updates to system management services that improve Stability.

[Auto] Updates to system management services that improve Device Performance.

Utilities

[Auto, PC, Phone, TV, Wear] New developer features for Google and third party app developers to support Utilities related processes in their apps.

Wallet

[Phone] You can now use Traveler QR in Google Wallet.

[Phone] You can now add Matter Aliro-compatible single-family residential keys to Google Wallet with Google Home.

Google Play Store v54.0 (2026-11-09)

[Phone] You can now find contextual AI suggestion chips on Google Play single-event LiveOp Event Details Pages.

[Phone] Delivers real-time updates of player sign-in/sign-out state for Play Games Services to Play Store.

[Phone] This update allows select users to receive Play Points promotions for new subscriptions on the Play Store.

Google Play services v26.43 (2026-11-02)

Account Management

[Phone] You can now access the Android Family Hub, a dedicated space for family management tools in Android Settings.

Developer Services

[Phone] New developer features for Google and third party app developers to support Location & Context related processes in their apps.

Device Connectivity

[Auto, Phone, TV] This update adds more quality logs for device connectivity.

[PC, Phone] Automatic backing up photos/videos from an Android to Windows using Quick Share feature.

Safety & Emergency

[Phone] Bug fixes for Safety & Emergency related services.

Security & Privacy

[Phone] Google Password Manager now allows you to manually choose which credentials to keep when importing conflicting passwords and passkeys.

System Management

[Auto, Phone] Updates to system management services that improve Battery Life, Device Connectivity, Device Performance, Privacy, Security, Stability, and Updatability.

Wallet

[Phone] Updates to Wallet loyalty cards.

[Phone] Bug fixes for Wallet related services.

Google Play Store v53.9 (2026-11-02)

[PC, Phone] With this update, you’ll get a reminder if Play Protect stays off for a while.

[Phone] With new at-a-glance highlights on game detail pages, you can quickly find gameplay style, review summaries, and gaming community activity before you install a game.

title: Nothing Ear (note) is yet another AI recorder, but with earbuds inside
snippet: Set to launch on December 8, Nothing has confirmed its mysterious AI product will be called “Ear (note),” and it’s an AI recorder with earbuds inside. more…
fullText:
Set to launch on December 8, Nothing has confirmed its mysterious AI product will be called “Ear (note),” and it’s an AI recorder with earbuds inside.

Update 11/25: Nothing has shared another image of Ear (note), showing how the case opens and the earbuds inside. The company adds that the audio quality matches Nothing’s “best in-ear audio experience,” explaining:

Ear (note) is a new approach to personal productivity, making it easy to transcribe, summarise and act on in-person conversations, calls, online meetings and thoughts – without requiring an additional device or new behaviours. At the same time, Ear (note) doesn’t compromise on audio, combining Hi-Res Audio and high-quality audio capture with AI that works in the background.

Introducing a new form factor, this is also the most evolved version of Nothing’s transparent design language. Built around an aluminium case with squared edges and a cool metallic finish, Ear (note) introduces machined metal and brutalist forms into Nothing’s transparent design language. Clear windows are inspired by the contours of topographic maps, revealing depth and dimensionality within the case. The TALK button and a new RECORD button draw on the controls on a retro Walkman, both positioned to be easy to reach and to provide tactile feedback when activated.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Nothing has confirmed that its new AI product is “Ear (note).” This builds on a pair of earbuds by turning the charging case into an AI-powered recorder.

The case has a “Talk” button, like Ear (3), which can be used to record your own voice, where a record button enables the ability to “record and transcribe conversations.” Ear (3a)’s ability to record audio from the earbuds will also carry over to Ear (note), giving the product the ability to record both conversations in person and over the phone. 

	

Nothing is entering a crowded market here with products from Plaud, Amazon, and countless others already offering AI recording/transcribing products, but building in earbuds is indeed a unique selling point. 

Nothing Ear (note) is launching on December 8, though pricing is unclear. Pei’s comments suggest a subscription will be used in some capacity.

More on Nothing:

Nothing reportedly launching two pairs of smart glasses, one with barely any AI

Nothing starts rolling out stable Android 17 update to Phone (3)

Nothing Headphone (1) Pro are $399 with better hardware, ANC, and audio upgrades

title: Nvidia proves it’s too big to fail
snippet: Good morning. Today I’m deciding whether the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer passes the “people just standing around” test, trying the new Material 3 Expressive Claude app on my Android devices, and stocking up on discounted XTEINK e-readers for Christmas gifts. more…
fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m deciding whether the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer passes the “people just standing around” test, trying the new Material 3 Expressive Claude app on my Android devices, and stocking up on discounted XTEINK e-readers for Christmas gifts.

Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Eleven days after leaving Nvidia, Jensen Huang is back as president, CEO, and a board director. The board voted unanimously to reinstate him on Monday, saying it was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead following a series of meetings. It also said input from senior levels of the US government left it confident that his reinstatement poses no national security risk.

	

I didn’t see this coming. Huang was dishonest to the public and to his board. He admitted to having affairs not only with an alleged Chinese spy, but also with an employee who directly reported to him. He is accused of facilitating the sale of Nvidia AI chips to companies like Megaspeed that knowingly purchased them with the intention of smuggling them into China, a contravention of US trade restrictions.

As recently as November 17th, the board chair, Harvey Jones, reiterated that the company had no intention of bringing back Huang as CEO. But things changed quickly on Sunday as President Trump reportedly reassured the board that Huang’s reinstatement posed no security risk to US intelligence, something that the new Democratic-led Congress will be sure to test via repeated subpoenas in the new year.

As Huang walked into the atrium at Nvidia’s headquarters, staff gathered around to cheer his return, and he addressed the crowd by saying he would be a “better CEO the second time around,” as if 11 days of unemployment had given him sufficient time to evaluate his past behavior.

Nvidia’s stock was up over 30% on Monday, rebounding from a disastrous end to last week that wiped out $4 trillion in Nasdaq value. It’s hard not to see Huang’s return as a direct response to this short-term disruption, which also hinted at a much more serious correction in the stock market. Nvidia’s stock had already fallen 24% between the day Huang resigned and Friday’s crunch, and with looming regulation from Congress in 2027, a rudderless AI industry could have been disastrous for the US economy writ large.

Though things may appear to be back to normal, or as normal as possible given the insanity of the past couple of weeks, Huang has returned to a very different trade environment. While he was away, Nvidia’s board formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to investigate whether the company’s actions violated any US embargoes. And as part of Huang’s return, Nvidia has committed to hiring its first chief compliance officer, an executive who will ostensibly not report directly to the CEO.

I was pretty gobsmacked when I saw the news of Huang’s return come across the wire at 9am ET yesterday. I’m still wrapping my head around it. Is Nvidia too big to fail, or just a symptom of a larger interdependency between the US executive branch and Big Tech? Huang promises to be a better leader this time around, but to whom: his employees, his customers, or his shareholders? Because he appears to be a very different person to each of those groups.

✉️ Inbox

In Ben’s Weekender essay, he speaks the truth: The Google Home app is better than Nest alone ever was, mostly.

Motorola Razr Flex leaks in real life with Fold 8 and iPhone Duo shape, mystery chipset. Based on the tepid reception to the Signature 27 and its $1,600 price, I have low expectations for this one, but Motorola knows how to make a good foldable.

Motorola’s iPhone Duo competitor, Razr Flex, leaks in detailed images [Gallery]

Gemini app for Mac adds computer use to control desktop apps. It took its sweet time, but Gemini now competes directly with Claude and ChatGPT where it counts: being able to accidentally delete all of your files.

Google homepage rolling out AI-focused redesign that includes your Gemini chats. This is a bigger deal than it lets on, since it’s the next step in Search’s inevitable slide into obscurity.

Google’s 3D emoji has wild Android spec requirements: 10GB of free space, 6GB RAM. Most Android phones have these specs now, so I disagree that the requirements are “wild.” But do we really need emoji that go this hard?

Google Search adds a clever Easter egg for Robert Pattinson’s James Bond casting. Cute.

Alleged Pixel 11 Pro prototype had HiLight and a temperature sensor. I return to my theory that it was price, not usage, that killed the Pixel’s temperature sensor.

Expect Samsung’s good-value Galaxy devices to get more expensive, report says. The cheap phone is dead, dead, dead.

Google Pixel held its ground in the US despite a middling Pixel 11 launch. What is considered a good Pixel launch anymore?

Hands-on: Sony’s Walkman-revival USB-C headphones are back in stock and worth a look. I can’t justify these terrible-sounding headphones, but damn do they bring back some memories.

Clicks Communicator hits a supply chain snag, and it isn’t because of RAM. Click, click, boom.

Google retiring Nest app and Google Assistant on speakers, displays in 2027. I know the “Killed by Google” folks are going to be all over this, but this announcement has been inevitable for two years.

Google Health 5.13 rolling out: Improved food search, more swimming controls

Google Health update fixes my biggest Fitbit Air complaint with ‘in-progress’ workout card

Samsung might copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island soon, but it actually looks good [Video]. I’m not mad about this; the Dynamic Island is a great feature that has changed how useful ongoing notifications are.

‘Galaxy Watch 10’ won’t launch in 2027 as Samsung tries to slow RAMageddon losses. I think Samsung’s phones should take a year off, too.

This Fitbit Air app buzzes your wrist with phone notifications, finds a lost tracker, more. I wear my Fitbit Air to avoid all of these things, but you do you, I guess.

Kodak SlideTag is a $35 Android & iPhone tracker with an E-Ink display to show your photos and more [Gallery]. Oh. My. Goodness. I’m buying 20 of these.

Gemini 4 Carbon is now available in Google Antigravity for AI Pro. Gemini 4 Carbon isn’t getting the same positive reception as its little brother, Neon, but it’s still a very good near-SOTA model, and now it’s available to the rest of us.

🛍️ Black Friday: the deals worth a look

Since it’s Black Friday week, I figured I’d round up some of the best deals we’ve found so far.

A discounted Pixel: The Pixel 10 at $600 is a really good deal. Recent software updates have closed some of the feature gaps with the Pixel 11, and the hardware is still solid even a year after launch. If you want better cameras, the Pixel 11 Pro at $749 is an absolute steal.

The gaming-tablet deal: The Legion Tab Gen 5 at $599 makes much more sense than it did at $899: an 8.8-inch 165Hz display, a 12GB/256GB configuration, and an included folio. It’s a good fit for someone specifically seeking a compact Android gaming machine. 

The last-generation watch: The 40mm Galaxy Watch 8 at $199 is the sort of older smartwatch worth considering when annual upgrades are modest. And because the Watch 9 is basically identical, I’d go for the Watch 8. If you are looking at Samsung’s latest and greatest, the Galaxy Watch 9 is $379 with a free $50 Amazon gift card, which is a decent deal, too.

A deal on the year’s best Android foldable: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is showing up at $1,499.99 for some lucky shoppers and $1,549.99 for the rest. Either way, it’s Samsung’s best product of 2026, and my current favorite gadget.

Some more great Black Friday deals:

This portable monitor is great for DroidDeck, and now it’s down to $85

First Googlebook discount takes $300 off HP flagship for Black Friday

Keychron’s keyboards and dock are perfect desk accessories, and they’re up to $48 off

Give your eyes (and wallet) the break they need with these TCL NXTPAPER Black Friday deals

Just $161 reclaims all that space GTA VI stole on your PS5 with this M2 SSD deal

Waterdrop Filter’s Black Friday sale brings big savings on under-sink, countertop, and whole-home systems*

The two best kids’ smartwatches are $50-$64 off ahead of Black Friday

Nintendo Switch 2-ready smart glasses from Viture are at their lowest price ever (up to $160 off)

Pixel Watch 4 & 5’s handy USB-C travel charger drops to $18.99

You’ll be aura farming with this amazing $100-off Oura Ring 5 deal

Boox is giving away my favorite e-reader during Black Friday

TCL’s Picture Frame TVs with Google TV are up to $800 off this week

*Sponsored

➡️ FWD:

Google’s latest mid-sized sedan AI model is taking the world by storm. Gemini 4 Neon is technically the middle sibling in Google’s lineup, with Carbon at the top and Hydrogen at the bottom, but everyone seems to agree it absolutely cooks.

If you’ve spent any time on X over the past few days (I hate myself for writing that), you’ll likely have seen an uptick in fervor over Google’s latest model, which seems to outperform Claude Opus 5.5, and even Gemini 4 Carbon itself, in many benchmarks and real-world tests. Even Google is providing some helpful guidance about when to use one or the other.

One thing I’ve read again and again about Neon is how adept it is at writing. I’m of two minds about this: the better an AI gets at doing my job, the less necessary I am at said job. On the other hand, I’m so tired of obvious AI slop that a model that actually writes well sounds like a relief. At least when I’m unemployed, I won’t be yelling at the screen all day about why the robot yet again used negative parallelism.

I didn’t get to play much GTA VI over the weekend, but I know a few (million) people who did. Publisher Take-Two says the game generated $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales. That’s an incredible number in any industry, but a truly mind-blowing one in the video game world. Rockstar also released its first patch for the game on Monday to fix a modest number of bugs with the launch code.

If you follow open-weight AI models, you’ll likely have heard of how influential Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 was when it launched in June. Now the company has released GLM-5.4, and it’s novel as much for its architecture as it is for its benchmarks.

Its Loop Transformer reuses a block of layers to do more computation without adding parameters. The company is pitching applications beyond software, including games, visual work, and CAD. The 750-million-parameter model reportedly performs at the level of a 2-3 trillion parameter non-looping equivalent, but we’re still waiting on a broader release for real-world testing.

In browser news, Ladybird’s first public alpha is now downloadable for macOS and Linux. It’s built with a brand-new engine that eschews many of the legacy decisions made by Google’s Chromium team. And the project has the backing of big names like Shopify, Cloudflare, and Proton. It’s still pretty rough, and features are paltry, but any new competition in the browser space is a win in my book.

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. I’ll talk to you on Thursday.

—Daniel

title: PrismML’s Bonsai 2.5 brings better coding and tool use to on-device AI
snippet: Back in July, PrismML claimed its roughly 4 GB, 1-bit Bonsai 27B was the first AI model of its size to run on an iPhone. Now PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an update to the model it introduced in September. more…
fullText:
Back in July, PrismML claimed its roughly 4 GB, 1-bit Bonsai 27B was the first AI model of its size to run on an iPhone. Now PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an update to the model it introduced in September.

The startup also drew attention when CEO Babak Hassibi told CNBC that Apple was evaluating its technology, as we reported at the time.

The new model is based on Qwen3.8 27B and keeps the same 5.9 GB footprint in its most compact format. This time, PrismML focused on helping the model handle longer tasks, including figuring out what to do when a tool returns an unexpected result or a step fails.

Bonsai 2.5 improved on six of the seven benchmarks PrismML highlights. Its SWE-bench Verified coding score rose from 60.8 to 75.6, while its AppWorld tool-use score jumped from 51.2 to 90.5. LiveCodeBench v6 dipped from 83.8 to 83.0.

What could that look like on a Mac? A coding assistant could inspect a private project, make a change, run the tests, and use the results to revise its fix. A document app could summarize a folder of sensitive files while keeping the processing on the device.

PrismML says Bonsai 2.5 runs on Mac, iPhone, and iPad through MLX. Its Apple silicon package is about 8.9 GB, and the model card walks through setup on a Mac. The weights are available for free under Apache 2.0.

For a closer look at how the model was compressed and tested, read PrismML’s technical white paper.

MacBook Neo sees early Black Friday deal

title: Anthropic just gave Claude users a new way to make Mac apps
snippet: Use Claude on Mac or Windows? Anthropic just released a new way to make personalized desktop apps using AI tools. more…
fullText:
Use Claude on Mac or Windows? Anthropic just released a new way to make personalized desktop apps using AI tools. 

Claude now lets you turn custom tools into personal desktop apps for Mac and Windows

“Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The “Install as app” feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows,” Anthropic says.

“When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.”

Additionally, Anthropic says apps made with this method can benefit from Claude connectors. Claude usage is tied to desktop apps made with artifacts. 

This form of Claude-created app is capable of sending notifications, adding items to the menu bar, and having its own permissions.

You can learn much more about the new system here. This is the second Claude update this week made specifically for builders.

title: Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are Everywhere
snippet: AI is rewriting the web in its own imperfect image, making software flaws easier to find and easier to exploit, while introducing plenty of its own imperfections.
fullText:
I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.

Microsoft Outlook? Broken, for a bit. Air traffic control? Had some issues. Bank with Chase? Monday was not great. But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto. I am almost certainly forgetting some.

Something must be behind all of this, you might think — a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet? But the answer is more complicated than that. All of these issues, and the ones that will happen after I write this, are probably unconnected, at least in the concrete sense. But they exist in a world where the infrastructure of the internet and the whole human world it undergirds looks increasingly precarious. 

			

More from CNET

Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counteradversary operations at cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, called last month “Black October.” This month? “Blacker November.” December probably isn’t looking great.

“This is not getting better, unfortunately,” Meyers told me.

One big reason for all of this, although not the only one, is artificial intelligence, but maybe not in the ways you expect.

Welcome to the vulnpocalypse

If it’s connected to the internet, it’s at risk. Websites, sure. But also utilities like power plants and water treatment facilities or, for some reason, grocery store freezers.

In the olden days, like six months ago, a hacker taking control would have required a fairly complicated set of skills, honed over a long career, perhaps in the employ of a government or criminal organization. 

Artificial intelligence, especially models developed and released this year, has changed things. AI has “democratized” hacking, cybersecurity experts told me. Things that used to require the capabilities and focus of a team of people with a clear goal can be done by a 20-something with an AI model and a specially designed program around it. And you don’t have to be a big or valuable target anymore to be worthy of a hacker’s attention.

A technical issue affecting air traffic control systems left airline passengers stuck in airports earlier this month.Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu/Getty Images

At the same time, AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities. These models and agents — essentially AI models that can do things on their own — can comb through websites or code and find problems that might have escaped the notice of humans. And they can do so more cheaply, meaning they can be turned on code that might not otherwise have gotten a close look. So many vulnerabilities are being exposed that it’s been given an appropriately bleak name: the vulnpocalypse.

Even that defensive advantage is a double-edged sword. Before, it might have taken weeks before a newly discovered vulnerability could be exploited. Now it might take days, even hours. If you’re responsible for a website or any of those things connected to the internet that may or may not still be maintained by their creators, you may not be paying attention and know you should update. You may find yourself liable if a breach leads to a leak of customer data. You may not have the know-how to fix it.

Another risk introduced by AI is that the technology, trained on all the lines of code its creators could find, is really good at writing code. Software engineers know this, and companies are now maintaining smaller teams of human engineers using AI to write more and more software. That code might be OK, but it might not be, and there’s a chance no human ever looked at it to be sure. 

Anyone can be a vibe-hacker

When I connected with John Strand over video chat, he was in Germany for a conference, and he was smiling. That wasn’t good. “You need to understand that whenever an offensive security person smiles and gets excited,” he said, “it’s bad.”

As owner and CEO of Black Hills Information Security, Strand’s job is to test systems for weaknesses, to think like an attacker and poke holes in a client’s defenses. He says he’d been getting a bit bored with the work after decades of the same techniques until the cyber capabilities of AI models started to explode at the end of 2025. New AI models were great at finding weaknesses in code, and AI agents could do the boring, time-consuming part. 

“You’re seeing something that can automate the kind of grinding grunt work of offensive security and bring that to a human operator much faster,” Strand said.

Things have only accelerated since the summer. AI agents are capable of more autonomy. And attackers have better tools to refine the often blunt instruments of AI models — harnesses. While an AI model can do a lot of things, a harness provides the tools and direction that allow it to do a specific thing more effectively. Think Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s Codex, but for hacking. Perhaps the biggest, most notable harness used by hackers is Artex, a significant-enough threat that the FBI issued a warning. 

In September and October, a hack of major South Korean banks led to the theft of personal information. Meyers says CrowdStrike determined the attacker was likely a 26-year-old in China using Artex. After asking AI how to do the attack, the hacker succeeded, then asked the AI how to sell the stolen data on Telegram.

“Anybody out there can now be a nation-state-level hacker just by using the tool,” Meyers said.

Despite efforts by major AI developers to limit who can access their biggest and most capable models, the hacking and exploit skills attackers need are within the means of models already in the hands of attackers. That includes open-weight models that hackers can run on their own hardware, away from the guardrails and peering eyes of AI companies and government agencies.

“The genie’s out of the bottle, and there’s no putting it back in,” said Gary Barlet, public sector chief technology officer at Illumio, a firm that specializes in ransomware and breach containment.

So many problems, so little time

AI-powered hackers, whether they’re individual vibe-hackers or government-backed cyberwarfare units intent on damaging critical infrastructure, always have an advantage. They just have to be right once, as the saying goes. Defenders have to be right every time.

The good thing is that the defenders are using the same tools as the attackers. And sometimes they have a head start. Programs like Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, OpenAI’s Daybreak and Google’s Fairwind let cybersecurity experts and high-profile targets like banks and healthcare providers have early access to the most capable models from those developers, often with fewer limits on what the models can find. The goal is to get a jump on patching and fixing the easiest and riskiest problems. 

It still might not be enough, and Big Tech leaders know it. In an October appearance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he no longer thought we’d be able to “just patch all the bugs” and that the problem is one that “is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders or countries or individuals, taken seriously.”

And defenders may not have much of a lead in patching bugs anyway, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the New York Times Dealbook Summit. Previously, when patching a critical system, you might have a week to test it before pushing it to production. “Right now the patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild,” Nadella said. “That’s going to create instability.”

The PHP vulnerability widely reported in October — with an urgent notice from the PHP Foundation for website owners to patch — stemmed from work through Patch the Planet, part of OpenAI’s Daybreak.

We’re getting increasingly used to seeing messages like this when we try to use apps or visit websites. But Microsoft Outlook is far from alone.Scott Olson/Getty Images

That’s just one high-profile recent disclosure. But there has been an avalanche of them. The National Vulnerability Database has received more than 10,000 instances of common vulnerabilities and exposures so far in November, after more than 17,000 CVEs in October. For comparison, in October 2025, that figure was less than 5,000.

“There’s effectively this big backlog of security issues in the open-source world that hadn’t been discovered until AI was able to just spend tons of time analyzing it and finding these vulnerabilities,” said Matt Wyckhouse, CEO of Finite State, a cybersecurity company focused on connected devices.

It goes well beyond open-source software. The connected devices Wyckhouse focuses on include things like refrigerators and smart home gadgets — the kinds of things that probably didn’t have to be connected to the internet, but are. The source code of the firmware and software powering those products has been seen by far fewer eyes than something like PHP, an incredibly common coding language used by much of the internet. The code running these devices may not be on GitHub or floating around the internet, but an AI model might be able to reverse-engineer it and find an exploit. And suddenly an attacker can turn freezers into ovens. If you think ground beef is expensive now, imagine what would happen if a major retailer’s stock of hamburger all spoiled overnight.

“Refrigeration has to work for our society to function, as it turns out,” Wyckhouse said.

Employees had to empty freezers at a supermarket in Sweden after a cyberattack raised the temperature in the freezers to 50 degrees Celsius. Johan Nilsson/TT News Agency/AFP/Getty Images

Wherever the vulnerability is found, it has to be patched. That’s where the backlog of issues is really wreaking havoc. Companies that create or just operate software are swamped with important, critical issues that have to be fixed now because it could only be hours before an attacker can exploit it. It’s why your computer and the software on it have to update so frequently these days. 

“It’s daunting the amount of work and the amount of time it’s going to take to clean this whole thing up,” said Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov.

And patching isn’t perfect. Sometimes it’s not a cyberattack that causes a system to go down but the fix to prevent it. Software updates are believed to be responsible for several of the recent high-profile outages, including Apple’s issues on Tuesday. 

Things get even hairier if the code isn’t great to begin with or presents new problems of its own. And with AI writing even more of it, that’s a growing issue.

How safe is that code?

In the backdrop of all of this chaos is the fact that software engineering is one of the industries most disrupted by AI. Models trained on miles of code are great at writing something that works — no matter how many holes are in it. And to CEOs eager to cut costs and boost their companies’ stock prices, the temptation is to lay off engineers and have fewer people use AI to do all that coding.

Big Tech has been laying off staff by the thousands this year. Microsoft’s October announcement that it was offering buyouts to 60,000 staff became a key talking point just weeks later when the system powering its Outlook email service went dark for a day. Might things break less often if more people were on hand to maintain them?

Several Apple systems suffered outages in November, within days of issues with the FAA, Microsoft Outlook, Chase and more.

“I wouldn’t be surprised if companies start to backtrack on that more,” said Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at the database security firm Liquibase.

Companies might also have more junior developers writing and releasing code that would have previously gone through senior developers, with AI replacing the productivity, but not the experience, McCurdy says. 

That means the problem isn’t just the vulnerabilities in existing software, but the vulnerabilities being written into new software or patches to existing software by AI. The same technology is causing the problem, providing the solution and complicating that solution.

What now?

The main thing we can do now is just… wait. Wyckhouse told me he thinks the next two years are going to be a period of growing pains as vulnerabilities are found and patched. The end result should be that everything is more stable.

“I think software is going to be an order of magnitude more secure by the end of the next year or two than it is today for this reason,” he said. “It will hurt a bit.”

Whether you’re an ordinary phone user or a major corporation, updating your software has become more important than ever.

“You’ve got to patch. You go for a flu shot, and you go and have your preventative healthcare,” Meyers said. “You need to do the same thing when it comes to cybersecurity.”

But consumers aren’t without power, especially when it comes to data breaches. If a company isn’t properly maintaining its systems and protecting your privacy or security online, don’t use it. Having your data hacked and compromised has become ordinary. We get letters in the mail saying someone stole data from our bank or doctor’s office, and if we jump through the following hoops, we can get 12 months of identity protection.

We don’t have to put up with it, Barlet says. “I think we need to start having higher expectations from the companies we’re consuming from,” he said.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Jon Reed
						

						

							Managing Editor						
					

											

								

											Jon is managing editor for CNET's news and AI coverage. He previously led CNET's home energy and utilities category, with a focus on energy-saving advice, thermostats, and heating and cooling. Jon has more than a decade of experience writing and reporting, including as a statehouse reporter in Columbus, Ohio, as a crime reporter in Birmingham, Alabama, and as a mortgage and housing market editor for Time's former personal finance brand, NextAdvisor. When he's not asking people questions, he can usually be found half asleep trying to read a long history book while surrounded by multiple cats. You can reach him at joreed@cnet.com

title: Pixel Weather rolls out ‘Report current weather’ to ‘improve local forecasts’
snippet: Google this weekend rolled out the latest update to Pixel Weather with a new reporting feature and small interface tweaks. more…
fullText:
Google this weekend rolled out the latest update to Pixel Weather with a new reporting feature and small interface tweaks.

On the homepage, cities that have active weather warnings no longer have bright red card backgrounds. The pill-shaped container retains its Dynamic Color theming with just the text of the warning in red. This change also extends to the card on the city page. Finally, the source, like “Google Weather,” at the very bottom is now themed.

Old vs. new

The main change today is a “Report current weather” feature to “Share the current weather condition to improve local forecasts.” The card appears at the very bottom of your current location and can be moved up the feed. 

	

Google says to “Submit a report if the weather conditions don’t look right.” Tapping “Submit a report” brings up a “Report weather in [city]” sheet. You can submit two pieces of information:

Current temperature: Seems accurate, Warmer, or Colder

Current conditions: Cloudy, Clear, Rain showers, Sleet or hail, Snow showers, Strong thunderstorms, and Low visibility

On the privacy front: “Your feedback, device location and some diagnostic information will be collected to help improve forecasts. This information will not be associated with your Google account.”

This is rolling out with version 1.1.20261012.x of Pixel Weather that widely rolled out this weekend.

title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
snippet: The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang's affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed's assurances.
fullText:
Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.

The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too.

The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.

Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch.

And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk.

“Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week.

The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade.

On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls.

Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance. 

In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week.

“When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said.

Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly, the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion.

Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year.

“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China said in a joint statement.

Rep. Brian Mast, the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has also demanded that the Department of Commerce share extensive data regarding its investigation into chip smuggling, including by Megaspeed and its affiliates.

The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3.

“Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democratic member on the committee, said in a statement. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.”

title: Google homepage rolling out AI-focused redesign that includes your Gemini chats [Video]
snippet: The Google Search homepage is embracing Gemini in a big way, with a new sidebar redesign that puts your chat history just a click away. more…
fullText:
The Google Search homepage is embracing Gemini in a big way, with a new sidebar redesign that puts your chat history just a click away.

Google’s AI ambitions have been anything but subtle in their integration with Search, but Gemini and Search have had some clear separations. But, with its latest update, Google is very much intertwining the two. 

Confirmed by Google’s Robby Stein on Twitter/X, Google is now rolling out a desktop homepage revamp that gives Gemini near-top billing. 

At first glance, you’ve got the typical blank canvas with a Google logo and Search bar at the center, but the new changes start with Gemini-powered shortcuts underneath for actions such as creating images, analyzing files, and “brainstorming” with Gemini. 

	

These replace the existing “Google Search” button.

Beyond that, a new sidebar pulls your Gemini chat history and tasks into the Search homepage as well as including a “New chat” shortcut and everything else you’d find in the Gemini desktop app/site. The AI-heavy adjustment is very perhaps one of the biggest embraces of AI in Search since Google launched AI Overviews and AI Mode. 

Stein explains this change is because users are coming to Search with questions that aren’t “one and done.”

People are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done – and in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.

The new Google Search homepage is now rolling out globally, Stein says, though we’re not seeing it live just yet on our devices. Sound off in the comments if you’re seeing the new look and whether or not you like this functionality.

title: TikTok is currently down for some users
snippet: TikTok loading slowly or not at all? The service is apparently experiencing an outage for some users. more…
fullText:

title: The Galaxy A56 is a decent starter phone at just $299 right now
snippet: If you are looking for a reliable, everyday handset without spending flagship money, Samsung’s mid-range lineup is usually a safe bet. Right now, the Samsung Galaxy A56 has dropped to just $299 on Amazon, which makes a sizable $200 dent in its original $499 retail price. more…
fullText:
If you are looking for a reliable, everyday handset without spending flagship money, Samsung’s mid-range lineup is usually a safe bet. Right now, the Samsung Galaxy A56 has dropped to just $299 on Amazon, which makes a sizable $200 dent in its original $499 retail price.

At under $300, the biggest selling point here isn’t just the upfront savings; it is the longevity. Samsung committed to six years of OS and security updates for the Galaxy A56, meaning this device will stay current and secure well into 2032. For a budget-tier purchase, getting that kind of software runway is hard to beat and only matched by Google with the Pixel 10a.

Hardware-wise, the A56 punches above this sale price. You get a crisp 6.7-inch 120Hz Super AMOLED display, an IP67 dust- and water-resistance rating, and a 5,000mAh battery with 45W wired charging, matching the charging speeds of Samsung’s flagship models. The triple-camera array, led by a 50MP main sensor with OIS, won’t win any photography awards against Ultra-tier phones, though it is plenty capable for casual snaps. Plus, One UI brings plenty of handy Samsung ecosystem features and baked-in AI tools like Object Eraser.

Of course, the Google Pixel 10a is the obvious rival in this space. If you can catch the Pixel 10a on sale around the $350 mark, its cleaner Android experience, seven-year update promise, and superior computational photography make it a very tempting alternative. 

	

That said, it hasn’t been available at that price point for a while and can only be picked up for $400 if you buy renewed. Which annoyingly means the Pixel is sitting closer to its $499 MSRP and has last years specs anyway, so in many ways that makes the Galaxy A56 potentially a smarter buy for your wallet despite being a year older.

In my opinion, for first-time smartphone owners, kids, or anyone who just wants a large, smooth screen and years of updates on a budget, $299 is tough to argue with.
